findings.title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert (TOCTOU race)
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts in a separate statement. Concurrent new anonymous requests can all observe count < deviceLimit and insert, so the limit can be exceeded by the number of concurrent requests. The limit is not enforced under concurrency, which is the core purpose of the feature.

findings.title: Count window differs from the window used in the update path and in the API
findings.body: The limit count uses [now-30d, now+1m] while updateDevice uses [updatedAt-30d, updatedAt+1m] keyed on the device's own timestamp. Both are fine individually, but the count also includes stale rows that the cleanup job has not yet removed (cleanup keeps 61 days), so the count is based on devices updated in the last 30 days only while rows are deleted at 61 days; the semantics of 'device limit' are inconsistent with the stored data. Worth confirming the intended window.

findings.title: Limit-reached is signaled via RowsAffected, which is zero when the row is unchanged
findings.body: updateDevice treats rowsAffected == 0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, RowsAffected returns 0 when the UPDATE sets values identical to existing ones (unless CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS is set), so an existing device re-tagged with the same IP and user agent within the same timestamp window is reported as limit reached and the request is rejected with an error. The error also misidentifies the cause, since a non-matching row (device expired/updated outside window) is also reported as limit reached.

findings.title: Device limit error now fails the whole anonymous login
findings.body: Authenticate now returns the ErrDeviceLimitReached error, so once the limit is hit every anonymous request (including ones from already-known devices that go through the update path) is rejected at authentication. Combined with the update path returning the same error for any non-matching row, users may be locked out instead of being served as anonymous without tagging. Confirm this is the intended behavior and that the error does not leak as an unhandled 500.

findings.title: Synchronous TagDevice on the request path adds DB latency and removes the timeout
findings.body: The tagging was previously run in a goroutine with a 2 minute timeout and panic recovery. It is now called synchronously with the request context, so every anonymous authentication performs DB writes (a COUNT plus an insert/update) in the hot path, and the panic recovery was removed. A slow database now slows or fails all anonymous page loads.

findings.title: TagDevice now returns DB errors but the caller ignores them for the device-ID path, and the ID-less case still returns nil silently
findings.body: The new 'return err' in TagDevice is only reached after tagDeviceUI, but tagDeviceUI marks the local cache before the DB write succeeds. If CreateOrUpdateDevice fails (including the limit error), the device key stays in the local cache for 29 minutes, so later requests from that device are skipped without retry and are not tagged, even after space frees up.

findings.title: Device limit is read from cfg in the service constructor but the store is no longer injected
findings.body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now constructs the store internally with cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit instead of receiving it via Wire. This bypasses dependency injection, makes the store impossible to mock in service-level tests, and the service's anonStore is now a concrete type while the API is passed a.anonStore, so the cleanup/ListDevices behavior cannot be substituted in tests.

findings.title: New device_limit setting is undocumented and not validated
findings.body: The new [auth.anonymous] device_limit key is read with MustInt64(0) but negative values are silently accepted, which the store treats as no limit (>0 check). No documentation or conf/defaults.ini entry is added for the new option, which the PR checklist requires.

findings.title: Limit test does not cover the update-allowed path or the race
findings.body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a second new device is rejected. It does not verify that an existing device can still be updated when the limit is reached, nor that the limit holds under concurrent inserts, nor the API-level behavior of the anonymous client returning an error.
